newsitem.title: USA: Court battles on U.S. tobacco ads may last to 2001.
newsitem.headline: Court battles on U.S. tobacco ads may last to 2001.

text.p: The court fight against the U.S. government's curbs on cigarette advertising could last until 2001, the heads of the American Association of Advertising Agencies (AAAA) said on Thursday.

The AAAA, tobacco companies and convenience stores challenged the regulations on advertising put in place by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) at a hearing on February 10 in U.S. District Court in Greensboro, North Carolina.
A ruling may come as soon as Monday, but is very likely to be appealed to higher courts.

"Whoever loses is sure to appeal to the United States Court of Appeals. And the loser there is quite likely to appeal to the Supreme Court of the United States," AAAA chairman David Bell and President Burtch Drake said in a briefing document released here at the group's convention.
"This legal process could take as long as four more years," the men said.
Cigarette advertising has been banned from U.S. television for decades, but the new FDA rules would allow only black-and-white print advertisements with tame graphics.
Billboards, sponsorship of sporting events and distribution of free cigarettes would all be banned or curbed sharply.
Tobacco advertising is financially important to magazine publishers and some sports, such as motor-car racing.
The FDA rules, just one of many legal and regulatory fronts on which the tobacco industry is defending itself in the United States, are to take effect in August.
Bell and Drake said Congress was likely to debate translating the advertising restrictions into law.
"The debate could go on into 1998 and beyond," the two said.
The two said the AAAA agreed with the need to shelter people under 18 from smoking enticements, but the advertising curbs violated U.S. guarantees of free speech.
